BBC News (Tom Edwards, Elliot Ball) — published 2026-09-30T05:18:02Z, confirmed from article metadata. Search highlights.
Pensioners in Worcestershire concerned. Burnham said it was a "good deal for pensioners". Experts calling it a "double lock" — does not take account of sharp year-to-year wage rises.
MARY DAVIES, 89: "I think it's wrong - people of our generation will be missing out."
BARBARA WESTON, 75, former retail worker: "The triple lock is very important - we've got a small pension anyway, compared to many other countries. We're not living life to the full as it is, because we don't have enough money - how is this going to change that? We haven't got enough in the pot to pay for everything we need. I don't think putting it into social care is a fair trade-off."
MARGARET SMITH, 89: "You hear so many stories of older people who can't afford to heat themselves properly or eat well - nobody should be in that state. I'd be concerned if we end up falling behind where the pension should be."
MAL FURLONG, 79: "I'm trying to be open-minded on whether it's good or bad. I may need social care at a later date, and that's what this is all about. So I've got to remain open-minded and let's see how it all works."
JOYCE PINFIELD, vice-chair, National Care Association: "We've been in a situation where politicians have been trying to 'fix' social care for 30 years, without it happening. It's a very difficult one for the government to sort out. We love the vision of a national care service, free at the point of care. But funding it will be one of the main problems, of course."
